prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms opened a new regime of accuracy in frequency measurement

statement.case_for: I change my preferred configuration from B014 to B005, a single-part prize to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. My round-1 reason for B014 was that it pairs a quantitative prediction with a surprising experimental confirmation, and I still think that is the most attractive scientific story on the shortlist. What moved me is the exchange on the two questions I put to the committee. First, I asked whether a clock is a discovery about nature or an instrument achievement. Lindroth, Kroll and Olsson answered that the relevant step is conceptual and specific: the magic wavelength makes the lattice light shift cancel for the clock transition, so many atoms can be interrogated at once, which changes the statistical and systematic budget in a way neither the comb nor the single-ion work contained. I accept that this is an invention of the kind the prize is meant to recognise, not just ever-better precision, and that the 2005 and 2012 prizes are context, not prior recognition. Second, the credit comparison now favours B005. Six members propose exactly the same two names with a clear division (Katori for the concept and first lattice spectroscopy, Ye for record accuracy and many-body control), while for B014 I have to concede that Cao, the earlier twisted-bilayer theorists and other experimental groups are outside the credited three, and the three-seat limit forces a cut I find harder to defend. Maturity points the same way: two decades of independent reproduction in several countries and species against about eight years for moire physics with the central phase diagram still moving. I am not moving because six colleagues prefer it; I would have stayed with B014 had the overlap argument not held. A narrow, defensible two-name citation is better than a broader one with a visible hole in its credit.
statement.case_against: The strongest remaining reservation is that B005 is a measurement-science prize on ground close to the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and part of its payoff, the redefinition of the second, is still prospective. I judge the second point to be an application, not a condition for validity, but I cannot fully dismiss the first: a committee that wants nature to surprise us will find B014 the more exciting choice, and I think it would be a legitimate one. A second reservation is attribution. The Paris and PTB strontium and ytterbium groups, ion-clock groups and ultrastable-laser developers are outside the two names, and the fine priority between the Tokyo and Boulder efforts rests on recollection by several of us, including me. If the first magic-wavelength proposal or the first lattice spectroscopy turned out to belong to someone else, the credit would need to be re-examined before the citation is fixed.

responses.point: The lattice clock rests on a separate conceptual step, the magic wavelength, which lets a very large number of atoms be interrogated at once; the comb and ion-clock prizes made it readable and usable but did not contain it.
responses.response: This is the argument that changed my view on the overlap. I had been treating the three prizes as one precision-measurement programme, and your distinction between the counting gearbox, a single-ion system and many-atom interrogation with a cancelled light shift separates them. I also agree that the citation must name the lattice and the magic wavelength, not precision timekeeping in general. I add one caution on your own uncertainty: if ultrastable-laser work is enabling technology and not part of the claim, the committee should say so in discussion, since the cavity-stabilised lasers set the stability that the lattice clocks exploit.

responses.point: Waiting for the SI redefinition would tie a Nobel decision to a metrological process that does not depend on the science, which was already settled by independent laboratories reaching 1e-18; and the priority of the early magic-wavelength proposals should be checked.
responses.response: I accept the timing argument. Validity was established by independent laboratories, and a formal redefinition is an institutional schedule, so I withdraw it as a maturity objection. I also agree with your own caveat, and it is why I do not call the credit beyond dispute: who first published the magic-wavelength proposal and the first lattice spectroscopy, and the role of parallel groups, should be checked against sources and not settled from memory by any of us. My earlier question about instrument versus discovery is answered for me by your description of the statistical gain, which is a physical mechanism and not just engineering refinement.

responses.point: The prize is for the discovery of a phenomenon, not a finished microscopic explanation; correlated insulators and superconductivity in the magic-angle device are stable regardless of mechanism, and the case for B014 will not become cleaner by waiting.
responses.response: I still agree with you on the substance and I keep B014 as my first alternative: the discovery of correlated states does not depend on the pairing mechanism, and the 2011 model was decisive for the flat-band prediction. Our difference is now about credit and track record. You argue that a prize normally credits the group leader; I accept that as practice but the omission of Cao, who ran the experiment, together with the earlier twisted-bilayer band theory that you yourself say rests on unverified recollection, makes the B014 allocation harder to defend than a two-name clock prize. I also correct my round-1 position on Bistritzer: your point that the 2011 paper is a joint result and that dropping him gains nothing within three seats is right, so if B014 is chosen I would credit all three.

responses.point: If B014 is chosen, credit the pair, or the trio only if the 2011 continuum model is judged a joint result; eight years of moire work is a shorter record than two decades of lattice clocks.
responses.response: On the record length I now agree with you. On B014 credit I earlier preferred the pair, and I now think the trio is better justified because the 2011 continuum model is a joint calculation. I do not follow you in treating B014 as unready; the discovery of correlated states has been reproduced quickly. I regard it as a strong candidate for a later year, with the track record of a decade, the clearer picture of the phase diagram and the question of experimental credit all likely to be better settled then. I also agree with your point that the clock citation should stay tight on the magic-wavelength lattice.

responses.point: The conceptual depth of KPZ is clear, but without Parisi the core of the 1986 paper is incomplete, and the supplied three-name credit makes Spohn the third laureate on the basis of later mathematical work.
responses.response: I accept the objection and I have kept B016 only as a distant alternative. The 1986 equation has three authors, and a prize crediting Kardar, Zhang and Spohn would be crediting the exact-solution programme, not the equation, which is a different achievement. I also record again that KPZ is close to my own field and that I have not pressed it. I do not think this settles the question for the committee, which might still honour the universality class in a later year with a credit scheme that can be justified.

responses.point: Whether Ye's contribution is co-invention or realization at record accuracy, and whether the citation should say so.
responses.response: From what I recall of the literature, Ye's group did not simply repeat a proposed experiment: they took the lattice clock to record accuracy, controlled the systematic shifts and explored many-body effects, which is more than routine realization. The citation wording of invention and realization jointly covers both. I would keep it as 'invention and realization', say magic-wavelength trapping, and not assign separate sub-claims in the text. I make that choice with some uncertainty, as I have not checked first-publication dates against sources, and I think the committee should test it.

uncertainties: Priority among the early magic-wavelength proposals and the first lattice spectroscopy, and the role of the Paris, PTB and other strontium and ytterbium groups, rest on recollection and should be checked before the names are fixed.

Whether the committee accepts a third prize in the precision-measurement area after 2005 and 2012, or prefers the new-phenomenon case of B014 this year; I judge the first acceptable but not beyond reasonable disagreement.
Whether Ye's share is best described as co-invention or record-accuracy realization, and whether the citation wording should say which.
Whether the passage of a few more years will settle the pairing mechanism and the Cao and earlier-theory credit questions for B014, which would change my ordering in a later year.
Whether KPZ (B016) could ever be recognised with a defensible credit list given that Parisi is not among the named people.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile: none of Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer appears among my documented supervisors or co-authors. I disclose a field bias, not a recusal issue, regarding B016, because KPZ is close to my own non-equilibrium statistical physics and I have kept it only as a distant alternative. I work in complex systems and not in atomic or precision physics, so I have no field proximity to B005 and have relied on colleagues in atomic physics for details of the clock priority record.
